A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dynamic-tokenization research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original XLM-R experiments on XNLI and UNER, Mistral-7B experiments on MMLU and MT-Bench, and an embedding-cache analysis.

after.justification: v3 retains original encoder and decoder experiments and reports additional multilingual MMLU results, vocabulary comparisons, and model/hypernetwork FLOPs estimates.

M1.justification: Batch-level BPE-style merging, pretrained hypernetwork embeddings, fixed or sampled merge-count adapters, and longest-prefix tokenization with ANN retrieval remain unchanged. The vocabulary-expansion method moves from v1 Section 3.3 to v3 Appendix C; expanded training and scoring explanations do not establish a procedural change.

E1.justification: Decoder knowledge-scoring coverage expands from English MMLU to Global-MMLU-lite in English, French, German, Spanish, and Portuguese. XNLI, UNER, MT-Bench, and the MADLAD-400 vocabulary-training corpus remain. The encoder language-count correction from 15 to 14 does not represent changed coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Figure 4a adds FVT input embeddings with original output embeddings to the decoder-scoring comparison. v1 evaluates FVT in encoder experiments but compares only original and hypernetwork embeddings for decoders. The other embedding, adapter, and ANN-versus-exhaustive comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: The reported five-shot MMLU template removes the topic preamble and context sentences preceding demonstrations (v1 Appendix C versus v3 Figure 5). The added efficiency evaluation introduces per-sample model and hypernetwork FLOPs across eleven compression levels. Newly disclosed training and index settings do not establish changes to retained experiments.

E4.justification: v3 adds systematic analysis of hypernetwork computational overhead relative to compression savings across five languages (Table 4 and Appendix E). It also extends embedding-control analysis to decoder FVT and tokenizer/vocabulary comparisons to English MMLU (Table 9). The fixed-versus-sampled merge and LRU-cache analyses already exist in v1.

E5.justification: v3 Table 5 newly reports Python, PyTorch, and NumPy random seeds for encoder, MMLU, and MT-Bench experiments. This is new seed documentation, not evidence of additional repeated runs. Neither version reports confidence intervals, multi-seed variability, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v3 reports new five-language MMLU curves, English MMLU vocabulary-expansion results, and FLOPs estimates. Table 9 reports 55.9% accuracy with 13.6% shorter prompts for the 1M vocabulary. Matched XNLI, UNER, and MT-Bench table rows remain numerically identical. The changed MMLU coverage prevents interpreting its replacement curves as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The tokenizer definitions, update-function equations, hypernetwork embedding equation, uniform merge sampling, ANN softmax formulation, and BPE merge-conflict example are retained. The expanded conditional-probability explanation introduces no substantive new derivation, assumption, theorem, or proof.

C1.justification: The central retrofitting, efficiency, and cross-lingual fairness claims persist. Decoder headline claims change from up to 40% reduction relative to word-level compression in v1 to 17% absolute reduction for multilingual MMLU and approximately 6% for English MT-Bench in v3. Large-vocabulary generation remains a contribution but receives less emphasis in the abstract and conclusion.

C2.justification: v3 newly attributes decoder degradation primarily to output embeddings and discusses key-value-cache compression. It adds near-linear FLOPs interpretations and explicit qualifications concerning hypernetwork accuracy, availability, training cost, and overhead. The requirement to know the input sequence and the bounded, static generation vocabulary were already acknowledged in v1.

D1.justification: v3 adds extensive LoRA hyperparameters, optimizer settings, precision and sequence limits, decoder generation settings, GPU/CUDA information, ScaNN configuration, and hypernetwork access and training-cost information (Appendices B, C, and F). These substantially expand reproducibility documentation. However, v1's footnote identifying the corrected MT-Bench source is omitted.

R1.justification: v3 adds work on tokenizer choice and limitations, including Ali et al., Bostrom and Durrett, and Dagan et al., plus Global-MMLU and softmax-bottleneck references. Some earlier citations, including Sachidananda et al. and Petrov et al., disappear. The central positioning relative to ZeTT and vocabulary expansion remains; publication metadata updates do not constitute new works.

P1.justification: v3 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, method explanations, and results narrative. It separates encoder and decoder experimental subsections, moves the detailed vocabulary-expansion method and discussion into Appendix C, and adds a limitations section and reorganized reproducibility appendices. These changes substantially restructure the presentation.

P2.justification: v3 adds an introductory English/Swahili tokenization table, combines encoder and prefilling diagrams into Figure 1, and relocates the ANN diagram to the appendix. It redraws the decoder comparison, adds computational-cost and implementation tables, regroups encoder displays, and clarifies compression captions. The existing cache plot and MT-Bench results are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important gaps in v1 through detailed reproducibility settings and quantitative accounting of model and hypernetwork computation. Multilingual decoder evaluation and the FVT control strengthen empirical support, while explicit limitations and absolute compression figures clarify applicability. FLOPs estimates still do not establish end-to-end latency, and the corrected-MT-Bench source note is lost, but the overall gains in experimental grounding, reproducibility, and clarity are substantial.
